citeAs: Dan Hendrycks, Collin Burns, Saurav Kadavath, Akul Arora, Steven Basart, Eric Tang, Dawn Song, Jacob Steinhardt (2021). Measuring Mathematical Problem Solving With the MATH Dataset. NeurIPS 2021 Track on Datasets and Benchmarks.
creator: Dan Hendrycks, Collin Burns, Saurav Kadavath, Akul Arora, Steven Basart, Eric Tang, Dawn Song, Jacob Steinhardt (UC Berkeley / UChicago)
description: MATH is a dataset of 12,500 challenging competition mathematics problems (7,500 training and 5,000 test) sourced from high school math competitions including AMC 10, AMC 12, and AIME. Each problem includes a full step-by-step solution written in LaTeX and natural language, and a final boxed answer. Problems are tagged by difficulty level (1–5) and span seven subjects: Prealgebra, Algebra, Number Theory, Counting and Probability, Geometry, Intermediate Algebra, and Precalculus.
name: MATH
rai:annotationsPerItem: Each problem has one difficulty label (1–5) and one step-by-step solution with a final boxed answer, as curated by the competition mathematics community.
rai:annotatorDemographics: For human evaluation, six university students studying computer science participated. Four participants are authors on the paper. The other two are friends or acquaintances of the authors. All participants gave consent. Participants had one hour to complete 20 problems without a calculator. Participants were offered remuneration but volunteered.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Problems are tagged by difficulty level from 1 to 5, following AoPS conventions. A subject's easiest problems are assigned difficulty level 1 and hardest problems level 5. For example, the first few problems of an AMC 8 exam are often level 1, while AIME problems are level 5. Each problem has a step-by-step solution and a final boxed answer. Automatic assessment parses the content inside the \boxed{} command and compares it with the ground truth answer.
rai:dataCollection: Problems were collected from mathematics competitions including the AMC 10, AMC 12, AIME, and more. Many problems were collected from aops.com/community/c3158_usa_contests. These competitions span decades and assess the mathematical problem-solving ability of the best young mathematical talent in the United States.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Competition mathematics problems from AMC 10, AMC 12, AIME, and other contests, sourced from aops.com. Problems are written in LaTeX and natural language, with figures encoded in the Asymptote vector graphics language.
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset is challenging even for humans: a computer science PhD student attained approximately 40% accuracy, and a three-time IMO gold medalist attained 90%. Large language models achieved only 3.0%–6.9% accuracy. The dataset does not include problems solvable by straightforward K-12 mathematics tools. Models are unable to effectively use their own generated step-by-step solutions at test time. The authors note that simply scaling Transformer models is not currently sufficient to solve MATH.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Problems and solutions are consistently formatted using LaTeX and the Asymptote vector graphics language. Final boxed answers follow consistent formatting rules: probabilities expressed as simplified fractions; matrix entry fractions encoded with x/y; other fractions with \frac{x}{y}; coefficients encoded without multiplication symbol; expressions with multiple variables in alphabetical order; polynomials in decreasing degree order. Equivalent representations (e.g., \frac{x}{y} and \dfrac{x}{y}, \left( and (, 0.5 and 1/2) are treated as equivalent. Units may be included or omitted; spaces are ignored.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is intended to advance machine learning research in mathematical reasoning. The authors note that even 40% accuracy for a machine learning model would be impressive but would have ramifications for cheating on homework. The dataset is explicitly not intended to train models that help students cheat on mathematics exams. The authors discuss that solving MATH with machine learning would be of profound practical and intellectual significance given the broad applicability of mathematics.
rai:dataUseCases: Benchmarking mathematical problem-solving ability of machine learning models; training models to generate step-by-step answer derivations and explanations; forecasting reasoning capabilities of ML systems. The authors explicitly state they do not intend for the dataset to train models that help students cheat on mathematics exams.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: None. The dataset consists of mathematics competition problems and solutions with no personal or sensitive information.

null_reasons.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Problems were curated from competition mathematics sources (AoPS), not annotated via a platform. Human evaluation was done informally with six participants, not via a crowdsourcing platform.
null_reasons.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: No inter-annotator agreement or annotation quality analysis is described; difficulty labels follow AoPS conventions and answers are algorithmically verified.
null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: No specific collection timeframe is stated; the paper only notes competitions span decades.
null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: No discussion of missing data handling in the paper.
null_reasons.rai:dataImputationProtocol: No imputation protocol described; dataset consists of complete competition problems.
null_reasons.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: No post-collection manipulation (augmentation, resampling, etc.) described for the MATH dataset itself.
null_reasons.rai:machineAnnotationTools: No machine annotation tools used in creating the MATH dataset; difficulty labels and solutions come from competition sources.
null_reasons.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: No versioning or maintenance plan described in the paper.
null_reasons.rai:dataBiases: No explicit bias acknowledgements or bias-mitigation design decisions are discussed for the MATH dataset.
